agent_notes: The packet marks חושה as Qere (Q(K)) without showing the Ketiv; I glossed the reading 'make haste' and could not note the written form.

The verb forms are imperfects that read as jussives (a wish), as the KJV, ASV and BBE take them; YLT reads them as statements. Wish is chosen because v.12 is a prayer and v.24 reports the same shame as accomplished.
שֹׂטְנֵי is a participle of the root שׂטן (to oppose, to accuse); it is rendered 'accusers' to keep the root visible. The noun 'the Satan' is not meant here.

agent_notes: סְפֹרוֹת occurs only here; the packet's commentators (Radak, Meiri, Ibn Ezra) take it as a noun 'numbers' patterned like בְּשׂוֹרוֹת. I did not rely on any other lexical claim.

Ketiv/Qere twice: the written forms הראיתנו and תחיינו ('us') are read as הראיתני and תחייני ('me'). The glosses follow the reading ('me'); Radak (as quoted in the packet) takes the written plural as the exile of the people. The note is in the commentary.
תָּשׁוּב תְּחַיֵּנִי is a verbal hendiadys ('you will again revive me'), but the literal layer keeps the two verbs apart, as the Hebrew repeats תָּשׁוּב before both clauses.

history.note: [consider] Replace 'for the reviewer' with a reader-facing phrase, and mention that the ASV translates the Ketiv plural. (PS.71.20 ASV: "Thou, who hast showed us many and sore troubles, Wilt quicken us again")

agent_notes: תֶּרֶב is vocalised as a Hiphil ('you will make great') without the usual ה; Ibn Ezra and Meiri, in the packet, both read it as Hiphil. וְתִסֹּב is read as 'turn about', with the object understood: to turn to me (Radak), or around me (KJV 'on every side'). The dramatic layer keeps both.
אֲמִתְּךָ is placed after נֶבֶל and can be read as the reason for the praise ('for your faithfulness') or as a second object ('your faithfulness'). The literal layer keeps it bare.

agent_notes: Revised per the reviewer request: the commentary and the תְּרַנֵּנָּה note now give Ibn Ezra's grammatical reading of the doubled nun (it makes up for the geminate root's lost third nun) and no longer speak of intensity or strengthening; the פָּדִיתָ note gives his reason for naming the soul (it rules the body).

STEPBible glosses כִּי as 'if'; I read it as causal-temporal ('for'/'when'), as KJV, ASV and Webster do. YLT's 'when' and BBE's 'when' fit the same sense. The verse ends without a verb for the soul: the line is left open in the literal layer, and the dramatic layer carries over the verb 'sing' from the first clause, as Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Metzudat David do (they supply 'will sing').

Ibn Ezra's 'ba-kinnor' ('with the lyre') is his own paraphrase and is not in the verse; I mention it only as his reading of the occasion. The Radak claim about exile and the Meiri claim about the depth of the heart are cited as theirs, not as the verse's plain sense.

agent_notes: Applied the reviewer's request: the commentary now says the KJV keeps the Hebrew's three terms (wicked, unrighteous, cruel) and only adds the noun 'man', turning the participles me'avvel and chometz into adjectives of one man.

STEPBible glosses מְעַוֵּל as 'wrongdoer' and וְחוֹמֵץ as 'ruthless'. I kept 'ruthless' for the second, but glossed the first as 'one who acts perversely', since it is a participle, not a noun. The classical commentators read חומץ as 'oppressor' by way of חמס/חמוץ (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion); that link rests on their reading, not on a certain etymology.
Radak's identifications (Absalom for 'the wicked', Ahithophel for the second figure) are his own reading and are mentioned only as such.

agent_notes: גוזי is rare. STEPBible derives it from גזה 'cut off'; Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion link it to Num 11:31 וַיָּגָז 'it burst forth/brought'. Many modern lexicons emend to גֹּחִי (Ps 22:10, 'who drew me out'), as Meiri notes. I kept 'cut off' for the literal layer with a bracketed 'brought', and rendered 'drew me out' in the dramatic layer.
